query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation because the chemically distinct and structurally coherent interfaces between layers act as effective dislocation barriers and promote local chemical ordering, which increases the lattice friction. This dual-barrier mechanism reduces the rate of creep compared to homogeneous, single-phase coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer high-entropy alloy protective coating composed of alternating chemically distinct layers with well-defined interfaces, fabricated using methods such as arc ion plating or spark deposition.
generation.intervention: Prepare coatings with identical overall composition in a multilayer architecture versus a homogeneous single-layer structure.
generation.conditions: Sustained high-temperature and moderate mechanical loading conditions that typically promote time-dependent plastic deformation (creep).
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces and corresponding regions of local chemical ordering at the interfacial boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Dislocation motion under stress is hindered at the interfaces due to misfit stresses and local chemical ordering, increasing activation barriers for dislocation nucleation and glide. This interface barrier mechanism slows down the accumulation of plastic strain over time.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature and load conditions, the multilayer coating will exhibit a significantly lower creep strain and delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to the homogeneous coating.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating with the same overall composition but without deliberately engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where the multilayer interfaces remain structurally stable (i.e., below temperatures or stresses that cause interfacial degradation or phase transformations) and for coatings prepared with sufficiently distinct and coherent layers.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of the interfacial barrier effect versus intrinsic bulk high-entropy alloy properties in suppressing time-dependent plastic deformation, and the magnitude of the effect across different alloy systems, remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings: one with a multilayer architecture of high-entropy alloy layers and another with an equivalent homogeneous structure. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature (e.g., operating temperatures relevant to turbine or engine applications) and sustained mechanical loading for an extended period. Use in situ nanoindentation or creep testing to monitor the development of plastic strain over time.
measurements: Time-dependent strain (creep strain) as a function of stress and temperature.
Microstructural analysis of interfaces (using TEM or SEM) before and after testing to assess interfacial integrity.
Comparison of dislocation density and motion in the multilayer versus homogeneous samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in time-dependent plastic deformation (i.e., creep strain) compared to the homogeneous coating under identical testing conditions, or if the interfacial regions do not show evidence of hindering dislocation motion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The Oxidation and Corrosion Resistance of AlCrNbSiTiN Multi-Principal Element Nitride Coatings

Abstract: Multi-principal element nitrides have great application potential in protective coatings. However, the investigation of the oxidation and corrosion resistance of multi-principal element nitride coatings is still insufficient. The synthesis and high-temperature performance of AlCrNbSiTiN multi-principal element nitride coatings fabricated through optimized arc ion plating (AIP) were explored. Leveraging the high ionization efficiency and ion kinetic energy characteristic of AIP, coatings with significantly fewer internal defects were obtained. These coatings demonstrate superior mechanical properties, including a maximum hardness of 36.5 GPa and critical crack propagation resistance (CPR) values approaching 2000 N2. Optimal coatings exhibited exceptional water vapor corrosion resistance (5.15 at% O after 200 h). The coatings prepared at −150 V had the optimal corrosion resistance, with the coating resistance and corrosion current density being 1.68 × 104 Ω·cm2 and 0.79 μA·cm−2, respectively. Strengthening in multi-principal element alloys with local-chemical-order roughened dislocation pathways

Abstract: High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 High-Entropy Alloy for Corrosion Resistance Coatings

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
